rv.q: Though some of the social attitudes and trappings show their vintage – male chauvinism and trimphones, anyone? – the script’s intelligence and passion shine through. Max Webster’s elegant production even manages a deft topspin of modernity.

And, in essence, this super-smart 1982 comedy represents Stoppard’s own wrestle with the same conundrum. It is given an elegant, mischievous revival at the Old Vic by Max Webster, with James McArdle enormously enjoyable as the pompous, acerbic Henry, a character for whom the term “mansplaining” could have been invented.

As the playwright, he gets the only good lines. The others feel like bit players, even Annie, who is a foil for illuminating Henry’s thoughts. Not every performance glows, and you never quite believe in any of these relationships, although McArdle makes his character believable and sympathetic, despite Henry’s incredible pomposity.
But looks are deceptive and so are the fast-talkingly faithless characters in Tom Stoppard’s 1982 masterpiece, here revived 14 years after its last Old Vic run.

In classic Stoppard fashion that last one is a brilliant observation, twisted from a line that originates with WH Auden, thrown around by the playwright as casually as wedding day confetti. It all sounds a bit heavy, doesn’t it? This is, however, an elegant production of a witty script.
I’m hazy as to the ins and outs of Stoppard’s lovelife during this era, but I’m dimly aware he was a naughty boy.

McCardle makes fine work of a man who loves the sound of his own voice, but whose confidence falters when it comes to talking, or writing, about true love. Where Wokoma is witty, weary and sarcastic, Powley is direct, emotional and restless, always longing for something that Henry can’t quite provide for her.
But then again, they’re not really trying to. Susan Wokoma is all fury as his long-suffering actress wife Charlotte, constantly snared by his sharp verbal traps.

What’s more crucial is the question of whether, in performance, his dramas also trouble the gut and the heart, and rarely more so than in the case of this brainy comedy of love, art and betrayal from 1982.

The play explores the ramifications of infidelity while broaching if a betrayal might give rise to a more authentic relationship. Though there are quotably succinct, comically sharp lines, the piece aspires to unfold the ordinary mess of intimate relations, the way love can seem fixed and absolute, yet has to be continually renegotiated.

It retains all the whirling wit of his early work, but its subject is the most important in the world – what it means to love and be loved. At its centre is Henry, a 40-something playwright, with whom it is hard not to think his author partly identified.
